newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Ousted Cambodia prince aims to set up rival govt.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Cambodia prince aims to set up rival govt.

text.p: Cambodia's U.N. ambassador said on Wednesday that followers of the ousted First Prime Minister, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, would amass troops in the city of Battambang and set up an alternative regime.

"We will take Battambang, the second city. We have disarmed more than 2,000 (opposing) soldiers," the ambassador, Prince Sisowath Sirirath, told a news conference in his government's first detailed comments here since the weekend coup led by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.
"This is our home and we will have a capital city...," he said, adding that Battambang would be declared "a city for the national resistence."
Negotiations, however, were preferable, he added.

Sisowatch called for the freezing of international aid -- Cambodia's lifeline -- and said the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) should do nothing to "make the coup a fait accompli." Cambodia was set to become a member of ASEAN, along with Laos and Burma, at the end of this month.

Sisowath indicated that followers of Hun Sen were attempting to exert power in embassies abroad. The ambassador's deputy, Ouch Borith, has circulated a letter from Hun Sen calling Ranariddh a traitor and accusing his following of widespread corruption.

Ranariddh, who was in Paris during the coup, was scheduled to see U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday. Annan has criticised the coup but the 15-member Security Council has been silent while key members deliberate.

"I have called on peace-loving nations of the world not to recognise the new coup leaders or the new regime, the military junta of Cambodia. They are not the representatives of Cambodia," the ambassador said.
He was particularly critical of Hun Sen's demand that other nations keep out of Cambodian affairs, noting that 60 percent of the country's budget was supplied by international aid.

"Cambodia is not an internal affair of the Cambodian people. Cambodian independence was born through the Paris Conference in 1991, was born through the open debate years in and years out until 1979," he said.

"The international community has invested so much effort, financial resources, human resources, peacekeeping operations...How can Mr Hun Sen say that the international community must must be kept out of the situation in Cambodia? No! It is very much alive, very much a fact," Sisowath said.

The United Nations and the five permanent Council members -- the United States, France, China, Russia and Britain -- helped launch a new era in Cambodia by brokering peace accords in 1991 and elections in 1993 that ended three decades of warfare, bloodshed and civil strife.
The United Nations sent 25,000 peacekeepers to Cambodia and afterwards organised a $2 billion reconstruction project.

Before the accords, all five countries had supported one faction or another, especially during the 1980s after a Vietnamese invasion that dislodged a brutal Khmer Rouge regime and made Hun Sen Cambodia's leader.
Sisowath said Vietnam had its own economic problems and would not interfere in Cambodia. "It is one of our friends in the region, our economic partner. It is busy doing other things," he said.
